# Airport Clinics Take Off: Travelers Find Quick Care Between Flights

*By Staff Health Correspondent*

For millions of Americans navigating crowded terminals each year, a sudden fever, a forgotten prescription, or an unexpected injury can turn a routine trip into a nightmare. But a growing number of airports are answering that anxiety with an unexpected amenity: the retail medical clinic.

Tucked between coffee kiosks and duty-free shops, these walk-in centers are reshaping how travelers think about health care on the go.

## A Traveler's Relief

Denise Halloran, a 54-year-old sales executive from Ohio, discovered the value firsthand during a layover at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport.

"I woke up that morning with the worst sinus infection of my life," she recalled. "I had three more days of client meetings ahead, and I panicked. Then I saw a sign for a clinic near my gate. Twenty minutes later, I walked out with a prescription and made my connecting flight."

Similar stories are becoming common. Marcus Webb, a college student traveling home for the holidays, sprained his ankle on an escalator at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.

"They wrapped it, gave me a brace, and told me what to watch for," Webb said. "I didn't have to miss my flight or deal with an emergency room. It was fast and honestly kind of a relief."

## Services and Costs

Airport clinics typically handle minor, non-emergency conditions: cold and flu symptoms, allergic reactions, minor cuts and sprains, vaccinations, and travel-related health needs such as motion sickness or dehydration. Many also offer flu shots, COVID-19 testing, and blood pressure screenings.

Costs vary but tend to be transparent—a selling point for travelers wary of surprise medical bills. A basic consultation generally runs between $75 and $150, while services like vaccinations or rapid testing may add $30 to $100. Some clinics accept major insurance plans, though many operate on a cash-or-card basis for the sake of speed.

"Predictable pricing is a huge draw," said Dr. Anita Rao, an internal medicine physician who consults for a national urgent-care network. "People appreciate knowing what they'll pay before they walk in the door, especially when they're far from home and their usual providers."

## The Expert Perspective

Physicians see both promise and limits in the trend.

"These clinics fill a genuine gap," said Dr. James Feldman, an emergency medicine specialist. "A traveler with a minor infection doesn't belong in an emergency room, and finding an off-site urgent care during a two-hour layover simply isn't realistic. Airport clinics meet people exactly where they are."

Still, Feldman cautions travelers to understand the boundaries of such care. "These are not substitutes for emergency departments. Chest pain, difficulty breathing, or severe injuries still require a 911 call and a hospital. The staff at these clinics are trained to recognize red flags and refer patients appropriately, but travelers should know the difference."

Dr. Rao echoed that point, adding that continuity of care remains a challenge. "We always encourage patients to follow up with their primary physician and share their records. A clinic visit at an airport is a snapshot, not a full picture of someone's health."

## Looking Ahead

Industry analysts expect airport clinics to expand as travel volumes rebound and consumers increasingly demand convenience-driven health care. Some facilities are experimenting with telehealth kiosks, allowing passengers to consult remotely with physicians and receive prescriptions sent to pharmacies at their destinations.

For travelers like Halloran, the appeal is simple.

"I never thought I'd say an airport made me feel cared for," she said with a laugh. "But that clinic saved my trip—and maybe my week."

As terminals evolve into miniature cities, health care may prove to be one of the most welcome arrivals yet.

*As Americans seek faster medical care, clinics in unexpected places are booming*

**ATLANTA** — For business traveler Marcus Chen, a sudden fever during a layover at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport could have derailed an important client meeting. Instead, he found himself in and out of a walk-in clinic near Concourse B in under 30 minutes, prescription in hand.

"I've never been so relieved to see a doctor's office in an airport," said Chen, 42, a software consultant from Seattle. "I figured I'd have to tough it out or cancel everything. This saved my trip."

Chen's experience reflects a rapidly growing trend in American healthcare: the migration of medical services into airports, pharmacies, big-box stores, and shopping centers as patients increasingly demand convenience alongside quality care.

## A Clinic Where Travelers Least Expect It

At the heart of this shift in Atlanta is **AirWell Health**, a walk-in medical facility that has operated in the world's busiest airport for the past three years. Handling everything from travel vaccinations to minor injuries, the clinic sees a steady stream of harried passengers, airport employees, and locals who find the location surprisingly practical.

"We're treating a population that healthcare has traditionally ignored — people in transit," said Dr. Priya Sharma, the clinic's medical director. "Someone might realize at the gate that they forgot their blood pressure medication, or a flight attendant might roll an ankle mid-shift. We fill a real gap."

The clinic reports serving roughly 40 patients per day, with wait times averaging under 15 minutes — a stark contrast to the hours-long waits common at traditional urgent care centers and emergency rooms.

For Denise Ballard, a 58-year-old Delta gate agent, the clinic has become a workplace lifeline. "Last winter I came down with a nasty sinus infection right before my shift," she recalled. "I got tested, got antibiotics, and never had to leave the airport. As someone who works here every day, having care this close means I actually go get checked out instead of ignoring things."

## Part of a National Surge

The retail and travel healthcare market has expanded dramatically over the past decade. Pharmacy chains, grocery stores, and superstores have all rolled out in-house clinics, betting that patients value speed and accessibility.

"Consumer expectations have fundamentally changed," said Dr. Robert Alvarez, a health policy researcher at a public university who studies care delivery models. "People who can order groceries and hail a ride in minutes now expect their healthcare to meet them where they are. Retail and airport clinics are a direct response to that."

Industry analysts point to several factors driving the boom: primary care physician shortages, long emergency room waits, and a younger generation more comfortable with on-demand services. ## Benefits and Cautions

Experts note that these facilities can ease pressure on overburdened emergency departments and improve access for underserved groups. But some caution that convenience shouldn't replace continuity of care.

"These clinics are excellent for acute, episodic issues — a rash, a sprain, a flu test," Dr. Alvarez said. "The concern arises when patients start using them as a substitute for a relationship with a primary care provider who understands their full medical history. If someone comes in with chest pain, we're stabilizing and sending them to a hospital immediately — we know our role."

## Looking Ahead

For patients like Ana Reyes, a 34-year-old mother traveling with two young children, the reassurance of nearby care outweighs the debate. When her daughter developed an ear infection mid-journey, the airport clinic offered peace of mind.

"Traveling alone with kids is stressful enough," Reyes said. "Knowing there was a real doctor right there, not a hospital across the city — that changed everything for me."

As healthcare systems nationwide grapple with access and affordability challenges, clinics in airports and retail spaces appear poised for continued growth. Whether they represent a lasting transformation or a supplement to traditional care, one thing is clear: for a growing number of Americans, the doctor's office is no longer where they expect it to be.

# At the Gate: How Airport Clinics Are Reshaping Care for Travelers on the Move

*Between departure boards and boarding calls, a new kind of medical care is taking flight*

For millions of Americans who spend more hours in terminals than in waiting rooms, getting sick on the road has long meant an impossible choice: power through the discomfort, or lose a day—and a flight—to an emergency room visit.

A growing network of airport-based clinics is trying to change that calculus.

## A Gap in the System

Jennifer Alvarez knows the dilemma well. The 42-year-old management consultant flies roughly 100,000 miles a year, cycling through connections in Atlanta, Denver, and Chicago. When a stubborn sinus infection flared during a layover last spring, she assumed she'd have to wait until she got home.

"I didn't have a doctor in whatever city I happened to be in," Alvarez said. "And the ER felt like overkill for a sinus infection. So you just suffer."

That "just suffer" mentality is exactly what airport clinics aim to eliminate, health experts say. These facilities—often staffed by nurse practitioners and physicians—occupy a middle ground between the high-cost, high-intensity environment of a hospital and the appointment-based schedule of a primary care office.

"Travelers exist in a blind spot," said Dr. Marcus Reid, an internist who consults for several airport health programs. "They're away from their regular doctor, they don't want to sit in an ER for six hours, and they're on a clock. We built something for that person specifically."

## Care Between Connections

Inside these clinics, the pace mirrors the terminals around them—brisk but purposeful. Common visits include everything from allergic reactions and migraines to blood pressure checks, vaccinations, and minor injuries.

Some facilities offer rapid testing for flu, COVID-19, and strep. Others coordinate prescriptions with pharmacies located just steps away, near the news kiosks and coffee shops.

For airport workers—many of whom lack easy access to daytime medical appointments—the clinics have become an unexpected lifeline, too.

"We see the gate agents, the baggage handlers, the folks who keep this place running," said Nurse Practitioner Dana Whitfield, who works at a busy hub clinic. "For a lot of them, we're the most convenient care they've ever had."

## Not a Replacement, but a Bridge

Health advocates are quick to note the limits. Airport clinics aren't equipped for true emergencies, and they don't replace the ongoing relationship of a primary care physician who knows a patient's history.

But for acute, in-the-moment needs, they fill a real void.

"Continuity of care still matters enormously," Dr. Reid emphasized. "What we offer is a bridge—so that a small problem doesn't become a big one at 35,000 feet."

For Alvarez, that bridge made all the difference. She was seen, treated, and holding a prescription within 40 minutes—still with time to make her connecting flight.

"I walked in feeling miserable and walked out with exactly what I needed, and I still caught my plane," she said. "Honestly, I wish these had existed years ago."

*— Reporting by Elena Marsh, CNN*
